title: Soft-landing continuity patterns for regional routing
content:
Purpose:
This note collects pragmatic patterns we can use for soft-landing (graceful continuity) during regional capacity pressure or model-family regressions. It focuses on routing/control-plane levers, model-variant polyfills, and a simple operational checklist for runbooks.

Context and goal:
- Problem: when a region is partially degraded (hardware failures, cloud throttling, sudden traffic spike) we need to keep customer-facing surfaces up while preserving SLOs and limiting cost blowouts.
- Goal: maintain a predictable user experience by (1) routing by latency class and fidelity expectations, (2) falling back to cheaper/compatible variants where acceptable, and (3) bounding cost and token-penalty via eviction/budget policies.

High-level pattern (summary):
1) Classify incoming requests into latency/quality classes (L0-low-latency, L1-standard, L2-high-quality, L3-batch) at the edge.
2) Control plane evaluates region health and capacity window; produces a per-route policy: preferred_region -> spill_regions -> polyfill_variants -> hard-throttle.
3) Router applies tag-based routing with a short-circuit policy: try preferred, if high queueing then try spill region using partial replica models, otherwise polyfill (quantized/distilled) with degraded-token budget.
4) Telemetry and SLI checks run continuously; automated rollback or canary adjustments if error rate or hallucination signals spike.

Key levers and how we use them:
- Latency class tagging (edge): attach a small header X-RW-LATENCY-CLASS. Use to decide whether to tolerate longer inter-region RTT for quality.
- Model family tags: model:falcon-40b, model:falcon-40b-distil, model:falcon-40b-q4. Router matches allowed fallbacks based on route policy.
- Regional spillover order: region-priority list with hot/cold preference and per-region cost multiplier.
- Polyfill variants: compact/distilled/quantized variants that are semantically compatible. Each variant gets a certified suitability vector (max_token_len, predicted-emb-quality, top_k-agreement).
- Eviction budget: per-customer rolling token cap during degradation windows to limit cost.
- Circuit-breakers: two-stage CBs (queue-time CB triggers spillover; server-error CB triggers immediate polyfill or failover).

Routing decision flow (simplified):
- Step 0: classify request (L0..L3), resolve customer tier (free / standard / enterprise), check pinned model versions.
- Step 1: consult regional health map (healthy/unhealthy/degraded) and available capacity estimate (free_gpus_slots).
- Step 2: if preferred region healthy -> route normal.
- Step 3: if degraded and request L0 -> attempt spill to nearest low-latency peer region allowed by policy (if RTT < threshold). If spill not allowed or fails, return 503 or controlled degrade depending on route SLAs.
- Step 4: if degraded and request L1-L3 -> allow polyfill variants with fidelity budget, or schedule to background batch lane for L3.

Model variant policy examples:
- Primary: rwl/falcon-40b-rtx
- Polyfill-1: rwl/falcon-40b-q4_0 (quantized Q4) — lower memory, slightly higher perplexity on long-form but works for most prompts.
- Polyfill-2: rwl/falcon-40b-distill — faster and cheaper but measured regression on instruction-following in our evals (~3.2% regen error).
- Hard-fallback: rwl/falcon-22b (different family) used only for low-fidelity completions or non-critical routes.

Quality control and telemetry:
- Telemetry streams to check: token_latency, queue_time_p95, model_agreement_score (polyfill vs primary on shadowed traffic), prompt-truncation-rate, user-facing error-rate.
- Shadowing experiments: route 2% L1 traffic through polyfills in steady state to collect model_agreement_score. Use as baseline before enabling polyfill in degraded mode.
- Manual signals: solutions engineering can flag specific customers to never be auto-polyfilled (enterprise pinned).

Operational safeguards and cost controls:
- Per-route budget caps: once a customer's rolling degradation-cost > X% of monthly committed spend, throttle or switch to ticketed escalation.
- Graceful token caps: for L2 requests specify max_output_tokens reduced by 30% during degradation.
- Fallback duration windows: default 15m probe/act window; requires 3 consecutive degraded samples before widening fallback.

Runbook checklist (quick):
- Detect: alert (queue_time_p95 > 500ms) and region_free_slots < 20%
- Mitigate: enable regional spillover policy (auto) and loosen polyfill allowlist for L1-L3
- Observe: check model_agreement_score > 0.85 (target) within 10m; if <0.7 rollback polyfill policy and escalate
- Contain cost: enforce per-tenant eviction-budget; if >75% of eviction budget reached, mark tenant for manual review and temporarily cap throughput
- Recovery: reduce spillover once free_slots > 60% for 3 consecutive probes; re-enable primary routing

Design notes / rationale (why this differs from simple failover):
- Prioritize small, reversible changes over immediate global switch: we prefer polyfill->spillover path rather than immediate cross-region failover which can cause widespread cost and cold-cache penalties.
- Keep fidelity bounded: explicit quality budgets avoid surprises where polyfill causes silent regressions at scale.
- Make policies declarative in control-plane: routes get policies as JSON (example in CON-plat-fallback-patterns) so SREs/product can tweak without deploys.

Experiment log (recent):
- 2025-02-10: sim-run (synthetic traffic shaped by customer mix) -> enabling polyfill for L1 under 30% degraded capacity reduced 503 by 85% but increased token-costs by 12%. Agreement score averaged 0.88.
- 2025-02-18: canary on customer X (enterprise-42) with polyfill blocked: 0 errors but 27% requests got 503 during spike; customer unhappy. Decision: add per-tenant opt-out flag and improve notification flow.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to encode semantic suitability thresholds for polyfills (agreement score vs absolute metric)? (TODO: define schema + thresholds)
- Should we add a mid-tier regional cache for KV/prefix caching to reduce token burn on spillovers? (Discuss infra cost vs latency)
- Where to store per-tenant eviction budgets and which UI surface allows operations to adjust? (JIRA-PLAT-987 assigned)

Links / references:
- CON-plat-fallback-patterns (control-plane policy examples)
- JIRA-PLAT-987 (eviction-budget work)
- github.com/redwood-inference/pr/204 (router decision refactor, WIP)
- slack #platform-failover (ephemeral discussion threads)

Notes to self / rough action items:
- Add a small simulator that replays real customer mixes with polyfill toggles (Marcus to pick up)
- Update console to show which polyfill variant served a given request in tracing UI (Elena)
- Draft customer communication template for short-lived degradations and opt-out flows (Samir)

Bottom line: prefer incremental, controllable fallbacks (polyfill -> regional spill) with hard budget and telemetry gates rather than global model switches. The control plane should own declarative policies; router should be lightweight and rely on short-lived probes and hedging rather than aggressive cross-region routing by default.
